name: Olga Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and fit timber balcony rails on new apartment building sites. My vocational trade certificate got me started, and I earn above the usual carpenter rate by taking exposed jobs, though I'm an experienced fitter rather than the foreman. I like a rail that holds firm; wind on an unfinished upper floor slows me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner repairs buses and our children are grown. We have about ten months of expenses saved and plenty of nearby builders with similar work. I use AI now and then to read product instructions; our retirement plan aims for regular site work to end around 64, but only if the statements cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the balcony crew a faster materials note is fine, but it won't fasten a timber rail to a real wall. The person holding the drill still owns the fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn above the usual rate because I take exposed balcony jobs, and my partner repairs buses. We have ten months of expenses saved, our children are grown, and I hope to stop regular site work around 64 if the income figures cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting the apartment balconies and check each rail fixing before handover. My partner and I will review our retirement statements this winter, then decide whether our target age still fits the household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about today's paid work. The pension check is just arithmetic until we know what it says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a balcony checklist miss a fault?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a bracket marked as fixed on the sheet moved when I pulled the rail. We replaced the balcony rail fastener before anyone stepped outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the retirement review decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would list expected retirement income beside food, housing and repair costs. If there is a gap, I will keep working toward the target or revise it, not stop because a computer speeds up paperwork.

say: **Balcony rails** still require a physical pull test after paperwork gets quicker.
The fitter remains responsible for **safe fixings** in a mild change.
think: My **higher balcony pay** and partner's bus-repair income cover current bills.
Ten months of **saved expenses** support a careful retirement review.
do: **Fit** apartment balcony rails and pull-test each fixing before handover.
**Compare** retirement statements with household bills this winter.
feel: **Calm** about present work, waiting for actual retirement numbers.
S0.quote: We replaced the balcony rail fastener before anyone stepped outside.
fieldNote: She found a **loose rail fixing** through a pull test despite a completed site checklist.
Her hoped-for exit around **64 remains conditional** on statements; the review is information, not retirement action.

steps.text: Fit apartment balcony rails and pull-test fixings before handover
Compare retirement statements with household bills this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can order brackets and book inspections before a robot can fasten a balcony to an uneven wall. I would try a proven ordering screen, provided the site fitter can correct the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid balcony shifts look safe for now, and there are plenty of other local builders. A wrong automated order could delay a railing and trouble the crew, but our household has enough reserve to speak plainly about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare the next two office bracket lists with the fixings we actually use. If the new AI order editor is adopted, another site proves its corrections and paid practice time is offered, I'll learn its edit controls before a live delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a hurried order, not my immediate wage. I like evidence from a real balcony more than a sales video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a wrong bracket list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the bracket order before the supplier packed it and send the measured anchor positions. A tidy AI list cannot hold up a balcony with the wrong anchor bolts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the editor works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see the editor fix a wrong bolt length on a finished balcony. If it cannot, the carpenter's signed measurements should control the next order.

say: **AI ordering** may change before robots fasten physical balconies.
A site fitter must **correct anchor sizes** before any supplier packs bolts.
think: My **balcony wage** looks secure in slower change.
Wrong **bracket orders** could delay work, though savings and local builders offer choices.
do: **Compare** two bracket lists with balcony fixings actually used.
**Learn** adopted AI order edits on paid time after a proven site correction.
feel: **Uneasy** about ordering mistakes while current income remains secure.
S1.quote: A tidy AI list cannot hold up a balcony with the wrong anchor bolts.
fieldNote: She learns **new AI controls** only after an adopted editor works on a real site and paid practice is offered.
Her **higher wage and reserve** keep this an operational concern rather than a predicted personal income cut.

steps.text: Compare two bracket lists with actual balcony fixings
Learn adopted AI order edits on paid time after proven site correction

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 may design the balconies, but capable robots around 2031 could fit them. The contractor owes us a paid crew plan and a safe test before it cancels anyone's shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 63 when robots do the fastening, roughly a year before I hope to stop if our finances allow. If my higher-paid balcony shifts disappear then, we will need a bridge. Ten months of savings can cover a gap in balcony pay, but cannot guarantee an affordable retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the site manager for written balcony staffing figures and robot stop rules. My partner and I will compare retirement statements with bills; if our figures are short and shifts are cut, I'll apply only to posted local carpentry inspection jobs with safe duties, regular hours and enough pay for our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible wage gap near 64, though savings and local jobs give me room to choose. I would not call an enquiry an early retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children the budget is ours to check first. They can offer advice, but I will not ask them to cover a missing year of site pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which safety rules should a balcony robot trial have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot trial should use a real uneven wall, a guarded area below and a worker with a stop switch. No one should use a balcony before a person pull-tests its fixings.

say: **2028 thinking AI** designs balconies before robots fit them around 2031.
Workers need **crew figures** and safe trials before shift cuts.
think: At about **63**, a lost balcony wage could leave a gap before my hoped-for exit.
Ten months of **savings** helps, but retirement still needs actual income figures.
do: **Ask** manager for written balcony staffing and robot stop rules.
**Apply** after income shortfall and cuts to posted local inspection job with safe bill-covering hours.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost shifts before affordable retirement.
S2.quote: Ten months of savings can cover a gap in balcony pay, but cannot guarantee an affordable retirement.
fieldNote: Her own **high-paid shifts** could realistically shrink at about 63, before her conditional target exit around 64.
The job application requires **short retirement income** and shift cuts, followed by posted local work with safe bill-covering hours.

steps.text: Ask manager for written balcony staffing and safe robot stop rules
Compare retirement statements with household bills
Apply after income shortfall and cuts to posted local inspection job with safe bill-covering hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 may draft the balcony plans and robots around 2034 may fit them. Five years lets younger carpenters learn a safe anchor check before their hands are off the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 66 when robots can do the fastening, two years beyond my hoped-for regular work. Our current figures look able to support leaving around 64, but I won't treat an estimate as a promise if costs rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I will review income and bills every year while I keep the present balcony job. At a local builders' apprenticeship association meeting I'll offer a practical rail-fixing session for trainees, but only if the association arranges paid trainee time and a safe mock balcony with supervision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about whether the retirement figures stay sound, not expecting a robot to cut next year's wages. The longer lead gives me a chance to pass on a safe habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would trainees practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show trainees how to set an anchor and pull the completed rail on a grounded mock frame. A trainee must never stand below a loose practice balcony.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the association lesson safe and paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the association for paid trainee hours, a supervised ground-level frame and a named instructor. If those are missing, I can share drawings, but I will not run an unsafe unpaid climb.

say: **2031 thinking AI** drafts plans before robots fit balconies around 2034.
A **paid safe anchor lesson** could prepare new carpenters.
think: At about **66**, robots may arrive after my hoped-for exit at 64.
Retirement still depends on **updated income figures**, not a guaranteed date.
do: **Review** retirement income and bills with partner yearly.
**Offer** paid supervised rail-fixing lesson at builders' apprenticeship association meeting.
feel: **Uneasy** about retirement estimates, with time for safe teaching.
S3.quote: A trainee must never stand below a loose practice balcony.
fieldNote: Her group teaching requires **paid trainee time** with supervision and a ground-level frame, so it remains a safety-conscious association action.
She treats **2034 as later** than hoped-for work, conditional on updated retirement statements rather than asserting continued site wages.

steps.text: Review retirement income and bills with partner yearly
Offer association rail-fixing lesson if trainees paid and supervised ground-level frame provided

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 may draw balcony plans, then robots around 2039 may put the rails up. If the figures continue to support leaving work around 64, this is the next generation's site problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 71 when robots can fasten balconies, well past my hoped-for exit. Our ten-month reserve and partner's work make that plan plausible, though I still need yearly income checks before calling retirement settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep doing current balcony work until our planned exit is affordable and review retirement statements with my partner each year. If we leave regular work around 64, I'll hand the anchor-test notes to a younger fitter before my last site day; I won't describe myself as a 2039 site worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the robot date being beyond my likely work, with a practical check on money. I can leave useful notes without pretending the future is promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a younger fitter check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the younger fitter pull the final rail after each anchor is torqued. A balcony handover sheet cannot feel a loose fixing under a person's hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make your handover notes useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The notes will give the anchor type, wall condition and result of the pull test. I would walk one finished balcony with the fitter before leaving, if our income supports the exit.

say: **2036 thinking AI** drafts plans before robots fasten balconies around 2039.
**Anchor-test notes** should reach younger fitters before older workers leave.
think: At about **71**, robots likely arrive after my affordable exit if figures hold.
The **ten-month reserve** helps, while yearly income checks still matter.
do: **Keep** fitting balconies on the current site rota until affordable exit.
**Hand** anchor-test notes to younger fitter before leaving if finances allow.
feel: **Calm** about likely post-work robots, subject to retirement affordability.
S4.quote: A balcony handover sheet cannot feel a loose fixing under a person's hand.
fieldNote: She separates **current work** from a conditional pre-exit handover, never claiming employment when robots arrive at about 71.
The **retirement target** stays linked to statements and bills, while strong savings and partner income make it plausible.

steps.text: Keep fitting balconies on current site rota until affordable exit
Review retirement statements with partner yearly
Hand anchor-test notes to younger fitter before exit if finances allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could take balcony shifts when I would be about 63, before our hoped-for exit. Written staffing, a safe robot trial and a real local inspection vacancy with enough pay would help if our figures are short.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tests a balcony rail after a machine fastens it above the street. A rail can look straight from the ground and still move under a hand. I want the pull test written into the handover.

headlineQuote: A rail can look straight from the ground and still move under a hand.
portrait: **Olga**, 58, is an experienced balcony fitter with a vocational trade certificate and higher pay from exposed site work.
Her bus-repair partner and grown children share a **ten-month reserve**; plentiful local builders offer options.
She uses **AI occasionally**, wants a tool proved on site and favours paid, supervised trade apprenticeships.
Fast robots make her **anxious** about wages near a conditional exit around 64; later robots likely arrive after work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring balcony robots around 2031, at about 63 and before her hoped-for work exit.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing**, a safe trial and a posted local inspection job with adequate pay would help if retirement income falls short.
